why: The statement is a single yes/no universal question, so a claimed nonrepresentable finite lattice answers it whole; both OpenAI manuscripts claim exactly that (any finite signature, no size bound), so each is scope whole. Neither has been digested: DeMeo, a qualified expert, engaged publicly but explicitly did not check the group theory (main paper) or the undecidability sections (companion), and the line-by-line reading was by Claude, which is not digestion; the partial Lean covers only the graph criterion. I marked them doubtful rather than credible because the load-bearing steps are unchecked, non-constructive, and come from a batch that has already had error withdrawals, but nothing specific knocks them down and DeMeo calls the result plausible. AI role is generated: the repository attributes the results to its internal model and the papers name no human author. The object is a counterexample (existence of a nonrepresentable lattice, non-constructively specified), direction refuted. DeMeo 2012 covers the finitely many lattices of at most seven elements, which is a finite census and so instances rather than case (close call; it predates the snapshot either way). Palcoux-Spiga bounds interval sizes and excludes no lattice, so none; its 'prepared with assistance' acknowledgement names no mathematical contribution, so ai_role none.
doubts: openai-math-206 duplicates the two separate OpenAI manuscript events (from a second, combined research stage); it should not be read as a third independent result. The researcher's manuscript quotes came via a model-rendered fetch and were not spot-checked against the PDFs. The model-generation attribution rests on the repository's general README statement, not a paper-specific disclosure.
